newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czech draft budget goes to final reading. [CORRECTED 16:40 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Czech draft budget goes to final reading. [CORRECTED 16:40 GMT]

text.p: Debate on the second reading of the Czech government's 1997 draft budget ended on Wednesday, and the balanced budget plan was sent for a third and final reading, expected to be on Friday afternoon.

Debate ended after Finance Minister Ivan Kocarnik offered a compromise proposal to a budget committee plan to redirect just under two billion crowns of spending in the cabinet's proposal to other areas of the budget.

After debate ended, the vice-chairman of parliament and a member of the senior Civic Democratic Party in the ruling coalition, Jiri Vlach, told Reuters he expected final consideration of the budget to begin on Friday afternoon.
The government draft plans balanced revenue and expenditure of 549.1 billion crowns, up from the revised 1996 balanced budget of roughly 491 billion crowns.

The budget totals are locked in by virtue of the October vote which approved the draft at its first reading, when four members of the opposition Social Democrats broke party ranks to help the centre-right coalition's plan survive.

In its second reading on Wednesday, parliament's budget committee asked for amendments which would have cut two percentage points off proposed spending increases across the board and readjusted state-sector wages in order to re-direct funds to other investments.
Any change to budget expenditures after the first reading requires adjustments elsewhere so that the overall expenditure and revenue totals remain the same.

Kocarnik, under pressure from the junior coalition partner Christian Democratic Union which objected to a two percent cut in the defence budget, offered a compromise leaving defence spending untouched from the original draft.

Kocarnik offered a one-percentage point cut to general expenditures while cutting planned increases in state-sector wages, except for teachers and constitutional-level officials such as ministers, members of parliament, and the president.
The full Kocarnik compromise would free up roughly one billion crowns (corrects amount from 1.7 billion crowns) for other various areas of the budget.

The other coaliton partner, the strongly pro-business Civic Democratic Alliance (ODA), appeared to have backed off suggestions that they might scuttle the budget because their demands -- including faster deregulation of energy prices and housing rents -- were not met.

Members of the ODA said on Wednesday that the party would support the budget as long as the coalition remained committed to price deregulation and other pro-market steps thoughout their current term which ends in 2000.
Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus's conservative governments have approved five straight balanced budgets.
The cabinet however on Wednesday announced steps to keep a revised 1996 budget within a deficit of 1.2 billion crowns, after revenues this year fell short of expectations.
The government said a package of spending freezes and accelerated debt collections from non-budget state agencies would keep the deficit in check.
A governemnt spokesman said that without these steps, the 1996 defict would have totalled between 3.2-5.2 billion crowns.
